inline.s: The Buddha said to Ananda: “Since Amitabha became a Buddha, ten small kalpas have passed. The land in which he dwells is named Sumati; it lies directly in the west, beyond a thousand billion Buddha-lands of Mount Sumeru from this Jambudvipa. The ground of that land is naturally of the seven treasures. The first treasure is silver; the second, gold; the third, crystal; the fourth, lapis lazuli; the fifth, red coral; the sixth, amber; the seventh, giant clam. These are the seven treasures. All of them together make up the ground, vast and boundless beyond measure, each set within the others and passing into one another, each blazing with light and shining into the rest — exceedingly soft and fair, beautiful beyond compare. That ground of seven treasures, throughout the eight quarters above and below, is the essence and savor of all treasures, naturally gathered and born by transformation. Those treasures all equal the seven treasures of the sixth heaven.

In that land there is no Mount Sumeru. Its sun, moon, and stars, the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, and the second heaven of Trayastrimsa, all dwell in the empty air. In that land there is no great ocean, nor any small sea, nor rivers and the waters of the Ganges, nor mountains and forests, streams and valleys, nor any place of darkness. The ground of seven treasures in that land is everywhere level and even; there are no hells, no beasts, no hungry ghosts, no winged or crawling creatures. There are no asuras, no nagas, no ghosts or spirits; there is never a time of rain from the sky, nor spring, summer, autumn, or winter, neither great cold nor great heat, but always harmonious, temperate, and evenly attempered — blissful and good beyond compare.

All things of ten thousand kinds come into being of themselves; food of a hundred flavors — when the mind wishes to obtain it, it is at once naturally before one, and what is not wanted at once naturally departs. It is like the things that come of themselves in the sixth heaven: freely, as one pleases, all according to one's thought. In that land all are bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and their lives last countless kalpas. A woman who is reborn there is at once transformed into a man. There are only bodhisattvas and arhats beyond number, all of them with celestial sight and celestial hearing, all seeing one another from afar, gazing upon one another from afar, hearing one another's voices from afar. All are seekers of the way and doers of good, of one single kind; there are no beings of a different sort. Those bodhisattvas and arhats are all of upright face and form, pure and incomparably fair, all of one color; there is none among them crooked or ugly. The bodhisattvas and arhats are all keen and wise. All wear garments that come of themselves; the virtue they hold in mind and the words they wish to speak are all foreknown to one another in thought. They always speak of right matters; whatever they say is always the scriptures and the way, and they do not speak of the faults of others. The sound of their speech is like three hundred bells. All love and respect one another; there is none who envies or hates. All speak according to elder and younger, higher and lower, in due order. In righteousness and according to propriety they serve one another as elder brother serves, as younger brother serves. In benevolence they tread the path of righteousness, never acting or speaking rashly. Admonishing one another, they teach one another, and let none fall into contention. Receiving one another in turn, all are pure in heart. They covet nothing, and never harbor anger, lust, or folly. They have no crooked thoughts, no thoughts of women. All are wise and valiant, harmonious and joyful in heart, delighting in the scriptures and the way. They know of themselves the lives from which they came in former ages, through billions of kalpas — the good and evil of former destinies, of what has passed and what now is — knowing it without limit through what Amitabha Buddha has taught. The lecture halls and monasteries are likewise naturally of the seven treasures: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and giant clam, each wrought together with the rest, exceedingly fair and bright, beautiful beyond compare. There is no maker of them, and none knows whence they come; there is none who brings them, and none knows where they go.

So weighty is the virtue of Amitabha Buddha's vows, and so good the deeds of those who dwell there. They discuss the meaning of the scriptures, expound the scriptures and walk the way. Assembled in the lecture halls, they are born by transformation. Those lecture halls and monasteries all have their seven-treasure towers, galleries, and railings. Again, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and giant clam are made into strings of jewels. Again, white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls are made into the netted canopies spread above them, and all of themselves give forth the five tones, fair beyond compare. The dwelling places of the bodhisattvas and arhats are likewise born by transformation from the seven treasures — gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red coral, amber, giant clam, and agate — wrought together to form their dwellings. Each has its seven-treasure towers, galleries, and railings. Again, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and giant clam are made into strings of jewels. Again, white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and mani pearls are made into netted canopies. Spread above them, each again of itself gives forth the five tones. In the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitabha Buddha, and in the dwelling places of the bodhisattvas and arhats, within and without, in every place, there are again natural flowing springs and bathing pools, all born together with the natural seven treasures — gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, amber, and giant clam — wrought together with one another. In a pool of pure gold, the sand at the bottom is silver. In a pool of pure silver, the sand at the bottom is gold. In a pool of pure crystal, the sand at the bottom is lapis lazuli. In a pool of pure lapis lazuli, the sand at the bottom is crystal. In a pool of pure red coral, the sand at the bottom is amber. In a pool of pure amber, the sand at the bottom is red coral. In a pool of pure giant clam, the sand at the bottom is agate. In a pool of pure agate, the sand at the bottom is giant clam. In a pool of pure white jade, the sand at the bottom is purple burnished gold. In a pool of pure purple burnished gold, the sand at the bottom is white jade. There are also pools made of two treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold and silver. There are also pools made of three treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, and crystal. There are also pools made of four treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. There are pools made of five treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, and red coral. There are pools made of six treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red coral, and amber. There are pools made of seven treasures together, whose bottom sand is gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red coral, amber, and giant clam. Among the bathing pools, some are forty li long, some eighty li, some a hundred and sixty li, some three hundred and twenty li, some six hundred and forty li, some a thousand two hundred and eighty li, some two thousand five hundred and sixty li, some five thousand one hundred and twenty li, some ten thousand two hundred and forty li, some twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li; and these pools are equal in length and breadth. Such pools are the bathing places where the bodhisattvas and arhats always bathe.”

The Buddha said: “The bathing pool of Amitabha Buddha is forty-eight thousand li long and forty-eight thousand li broad. The pool is wrought altogether of the seven treasures, and the sand at its bottom is white pearl, moon-bright pearl, and mani pearl. The water in the bathing pools of Amitabha Buddha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats is all pure, fragrant, and clean. In the pools there are fragrant flowers: a hundred kinds of flowers all born of themselves, each kind of a different color, each color of a different fragrance. Every branch has a thousand petals, fragrant beyond compare; their fragrance cannot be told in words. Those flowers are not flowers of the world, nor yet flowers of the heavens. The fragrance of these flowers, throughout the eight quarters above and below, is the essence among the fragrances of all flowers, born of itself by transformation. The water in those pools flows onward, pouring one into another. That flowing water is neither slow nor swift, and all of it again gives forth the five tones.”

The Buddha said: “Throughout the eight quarters above and below, in countless Buddha-lands, the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures who are born in the land of Amitabha Buddha are all born by transformation in the lotus flowers of the pools of seven treasures. They at once grow up of themselves, and there is none to suckle them; all eat the food that comes of itself. Their bodies are neither the bodies of humans of the world nor the bodies of devas of the heavens. All have accumulated the virtue of a multitude of good deeds, and all receive a body of natural emptiness, a substance without limit, beautiful beyond compare.”
The Buddha said to Ananda: “Suppose a poor beggar in the world were made to stand beside a king — would his face and form, his features and color, be like the king's?”

Ananda said: “If a prince were to stand beside a king, his face and form would be very ugly and uncomely, not equal to the king's by a hundred thousand billion times. Why is this? The beggar is poor and utterly destitute; his food and drink are always vile. He has never known a time of good food, and since his food is vile he cannot eat his fill. What he eats barely sustains his life; his joints prop one another up, and he has nothing with which to support himself. He is always lacking, with no store laid by, hungry and cold, fearful and wretched. This is only because in a former life, as a man, he was foolish. Lacking wisdom, stingy and greedy, he would not show compassion. He would not do good, love widely, or give in charity, but wished only to gain without labor, hoarding food and drink, eating delicacies alone, not believing that giving in charity would later bring its recompense; and he did not believe that by doing good he would in a later life obtain its blessing. Covered in ignorance and stubborn, he did ever more evil. When his life ended thus, his goods were all gone, and having never shown kindness or virtue he had nothing to rely on. He fell into the evil paths, and suffered there accordingly. Only afterward did he win release and gain birth as a man. He was born lowly, made the child of a poor family. Barely in human shape, his appearance is very ugly. His clothing is worn and torn; alone and empty he stands, unable to cover his body — a beggar born to it. Hungry and cold, in want and bitterness, his face is gaunt and mean, not the color of a man. Because of what he himself did in former lives, he receives this retribution. He is shown to the multitude, and there is none to pity him. Cast out upon the market road, exposed and wasted, black and ugly and utterly vile, he is not the equal of a man.

Why then is the king alone among men honored and excellent? Because in a former life, when he was a man, he did good and faithfully received the scriptures and the way. He bestowed kindness and practiced virtue, loved widely and followed righteousness. Compassionate and kind, he delighted to give; he did not hoard food and drink but shared them with all. He kept back nothing and was never contentious. Having gained such good blessing, when his life ended his virtue followed him, and he did not pass again into the evil paths. Now born as a man, he is born into a royal house. Naturally honored and noble, he alone rules as king, governing and commanding the people, and is their hero and champion. His face is fair and white, his countenance mild and handsome. His body is upright, and all revere and serve him. Fine food and good clothing follow his heart and will. Whatever he desires is naturally before him, and there is no contention at all. Thus is he beautiful among men, free of care and happy, his face radiant and bright — and for this reason, and no other.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “Suppose it be so. Though the king is matchless in beauty among men, if he were made to stand beside a Cakravartin king, his face and form would be very ugly and uncomely, just as a beggar standing beside a king. The king's own face and form are not the equal of the Cakravartin king's fair color by a hundred thousand billion times. And as the Cakravartin king is matchless in beauty in the world, if he were made to stand beside the king of the second heaven, his face would be very ugly and uncomely, not the equal of Sakra's upright and beautiful countenance by a hundred thousand billion times. And as Sakra, lord of devas, if made to stand beside the king of the sixth heaven, his face would be very ugly and uncomely, not the equal of the sixth heaven's king's upright and beautiful countenance by a hundred thousand billion times. And as the king of the sixth heaven, if made to stand beside the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitabha Buddha, his face would be very ugly, not the equal of the upright and beautiful countenances of the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitabha Buddha by a hundred thousand billion times.”

The Buddha said: “The countenances of the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitabha Buddha are all upright, incomparably fair, next only to the way of nirvana. In the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitabha Buddha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats, in the dwelling places where they abide, and above the bathing pools within and without, there are seven-treasure trees. Among them are trees of pure gold, pure silver, pure crystal, pure lapis lazuli, pure white jade, pure red coral, pure amber, and pure giant clam, each kind growing in its own separate row. There are also trees made of two treasures together. A silver tree has silver roots and golden stems, silver branches and golden leaves, silver flowers and golden fruit. A gold tree has golden roots and silver stems, golden branches and silver leaves, golden flowers and silver fruit. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, crystal flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. A lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots and crystal stems, lapis lazuli branches and crystal leaves, lapis lazuli flowers and crystal fruit. Thus two treasures together make one tree. There are also trees made of four treasures together. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, golden branches and silver leaves, crystal flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. A lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots and crystal stems, golden branches and silver leaves, crystal flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. Thus the trees of four treasures are wrought together, each in its own separate row. There are also trees made of five treasures together. A silver tree has silver roots and golden stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, silver flowers and golden fruit. A gold tree has golden roots and silver stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, red coral flowers and silver fruit. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, red coral branches and silver leaves, golden flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. A lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots and red coral stems, crystal branches and golden leaves, silver flowers and red coral fruit. A red coral tree has red coral roots and lapis lazuli stems, crystal branches and golden leaves, silver flowers and lapis lazuli fruit. Thus five treasures together make one tree, each in its own separate row. There are also trees made of six treasures together. A silver tree has silver roots and golden stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, red coral flowers and amber fruit. A gold tree has golden roots and silver stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, amber flowers and red coral fruit. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, red coral branches and amber leaves, silver flowers and golden fruit. A lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots and red coral stems, amber branches and crystal leaves, golden flowers and silver fruit. Thus the trees of six treasures are wrought together, each in its own separate row. There are also trees made of seven treasures together. A silver tree has silver roots and golden stems, crystal branches and lapis lazuli leaves, red coral flowers and amber fruit. A gold tree has golden roots and crystal stems, lapis lazuli branches and red coral leaves, amber flowers and silver fruit. A crystal tree has crystal roots and lapis lazuli stems, red coral branches and amber leaves, giant clam flowers and white jade fruit. A red coral tree has red coral roots and amber stems, white jade branches and lapis lazuli leaves, giant clam flowers and moon-bright pearl fruit. An amber tree has amber roots and white jade stems, red coral branches and lapis lazuli leaves, crystal flowers and golden fruit. A white jade tree has white jade roots and giant clam stems, red coral branches and amber leaves, golden flowers and mani pearl fruit. Thus the trees of seven treasures are wrought together, each kind distinct, row matching row, stem matching stem, branch matching branch, leaf facing leaf, flower gazing upon flower, fruit answering fruit.”

The Buddha said: “In the lecture halls and monasteries of Amitabha Buddha, within and without, the seven treasures and the bathing pools encircle the edges. Above are all the seven-treasure trees, and there are the bodhisattvas and arhats. In the seven-treasure dwelling places, with seven-treasure bathing pools within and without, the seven-treasure trees around the pool edges stand in many hundreds of thousands of rows, all of them thus, each of itself giving forth the five tones — tones fair beyond compare.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “As a king in the world has a hundred kinds of instrumental music, it is not the equal of the music of a Cakravartin king by a hundred thousand billion times. As the Cakravartin king's ten thousand kinds of music are not the equal of a single tone of the music in the second heaven of Trayastrimsa by a hundred thousand billion times. As the ten thousand kinds of music in the heaven of Trayastrimsa are not the equal of a single tone in the sixth heaven by a hundred thousand billion times. As the ten thousand kinds of music in the sixth heaven are not the equal of a single tone of the seven-treasure trees in the land of Amitabha Buddha by a hundred thousand billion times. In the land of Amitabha Buddha there are also ten thousand kinds of music that come of themselves, delightful beyond measure. When Amitabha Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to bathe, each may enter the pool of seven treasures and bathe. When the bodhisattvas and arhats wish the water to cover their feet, the water at once covers their feet. When they wish the water to reach their knees, the water at once reaches their knees. When they wish the water to reach their waists, the water at once reaches their waists. When they wish the water to reach their armpits, the water at once reaches their armpits. When they wish the water to reach their necks, the water at once reaches their necks. When they wish the water to pour over their bodies, the water at once pours over their bodies. When they wish the water to return to what it was, the water at once returns to what it was. Freely, as they please, according to what they delight in.”

The Buddha said: “When Amitabha and the bodhisattvas and arhats have all bathed, each sits upon a great lotus flower, and at once a natural swirling wind rises from the four quarters. That swirling wind is neither the wind of the world nor the wind of the heavens. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, it is the essence among all winds, naturally gathered together and born by transformation. It is neither cold nor hot, always harmonious, temperate, and evenly attempered, exceedingly cool and refreshing, fair beyond compare. It rises gently, neither slow nor swift, just right and well measured. It blows upon the seven-treasure trees, and all give forth the five tones. With the flowers of the seven-treasure trees it covers the whole land. They scatter upon the Buddha and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats, and as the flowers fall to the ground they lie four inches deep, exceedingly soft and fair beyond compare; and then the natural swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. Then again the natural swirling wind of the four quarters blows upon the seven-treasure trees, and the trees all again give forth the five tones, and the tree flowers all of themselves scatter upon the Buddha and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. When the flowers have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, they at once naturally depart; and again the swirling wind of the four quarters rises and blows upon the seven-treasure trees. Thus it is four times over. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some wish only to hear the scriptures, some wish only to hear music, some wish only to smell the fragrance of flowers; and there are some who do not wish to hear the scriptures, some who do not wish to hear music, some who do not wish to smell the fragrance of flowers. Whatever they wish to hear, that alone they hear; what they do not wish to hear, that alone they do not hear. Freely, according to what they wish and delight in, their vows are not opposed; and when they have bathed, each goes his own way.

As they walk the way, there are those on the ground expounding the scriptures, reciting the scriptures, preaching the scriptures, receiving the scriptures by mouth, hearing the scriptures, recalling the scriptures, contemplating the way, sitting in meditation, and walking in meditation. There are those in the empty air expounding the scriptures, reciting the scriptures, preaching the scriptures, receiving the scriptures by mouth, hearing the scriptures, recalling the scriptures, contemplating the way, sitting in single-minded meditation, and walking in meditation. Those who had not attained the way of the stream-winner at once attain the way of the stream-winner. Those who had not attained the way of the once-returner at once attain the way of the once-returner. Those who had not attained the way of the non-returner at once attain the way of the non-returner. Those who had not attained the way of the arhat at once attain the way of the arhat. Those who had not attained the stage of non-retrogression at once attain non-retrogression. Each expounds the scriptures and walks the way. All attain the way, and there is none who does not rejoice and leap up.

Among the bodhisattvas there are those who wish to make offerings to the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below. At once they all come forward, bow to the Buddha, take leave of the Buddha, and go to make offerings to the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below. The Buddha at once consents. Then those bodhisattvas all rejoice greatly. Many thousands of hundreds of billions of people, countless and beyond reckoning, all wise and valiant, each in his own company flying in pursuit of one another, all together scatter and fly. They reach the places of the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below. All come forward, bow to the Buddhas, and at once make offerings. When they wish to have ten thousand kinds of natural things, they are at once naturally before them: a hundred kinds of flowers of varied colors, a hundred kinds of variegated silk and brocade, a hundred kinds of kalpavrksa garments, seven-treasure lamps and torches, ten thousand kinds of music — all are before them. The fragrances of those flowers and the ten thousand kinds of natural things are neither things of the world nor things of the heavens; these ten thousand kinds of things are throughout the eight quarters above and below the essence of all that is natural, gathered and born by transformation. What they wish to have is at once born by transformation; what they do not use at once passes away. The bodhisattvas then hold these together and make offering to the Buddhas and to the bodhisattvas and arhats, on every side, before and behind, encircling them round about. Whatever they wish in mind at once all arrives. At that time the bliss cannot be told in words. When the bodhisattvas each wish to have flowers forty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Then in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air; the flowers are exceedingly fragrant and fair, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the natural swirling wind at once blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers eighty li across, they are at once naturally before them, and they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers all again come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the natural swirling wind at once blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers a hundred and sixty li across, they are at once naturally before them, and in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all again come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the natural swirling wind at once blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers three hundred and twenty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the natural swirling wind at once blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers six hundred and forty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again they scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; all come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind naturally blows the withered flowers away. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers a thousand two hundred and eighty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind naturally blows, and the withered flowers all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers two thousand five hundred and sixty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers five thousand one hundred and twenty li across, they are at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers ten thousand two hundred and forty li across, they are all at once naturally before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers fifty thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers a hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air the bodhisattvas hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers two hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats; when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers four hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each again wish to have flowers eight hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them. Again in the empty air they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. All come down from the empty air, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each wish to have flowers one million six hundred thousand li across, they are all at once before them; they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they all naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each wish to have flowers three million li across, they are all at once before them; they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats, and when they have slightly withered and fallen to the ground, the swirling wind blows the withered flowers, and they naturally depart. When the bodhisattvas each wish to have flowers six million li across, they are all at once before them; they hold them together and scatter them upon the Buddhas and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats, and the flowers all of themselves become one flower. The flower is upright, straight, and round, equal on every side, and flower upon flower doubles what went before. The flowers are exceedingly soft and fair, surpassing the former flowers by many thousands of hundreds of times. Color differs from color, and fragrance from fragrance beyond words. The bodhisattvas all rejoice greatly, and together in the empty air make a great chorus of sound, music that comes of itself. They delight the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas and arhats, and at that time the bliss cannot be told in words.

The bodhisattvas all withdraw and sit to hear the scriptures; when they have heard the scriptures they all recite them through and master them. They know the scriptures and the way anew, and their wisdom grows brighter. Then throughout those Buddha-lands, from the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the heaven of the Thirty-three, the devas and humans all bring down ten thousand kinds of natural things from the heavens and make offering to the bodhisattvas and arhats. The devas and humans all again, in the empty air, make a great chorus of music. The devas and humans who came first withdraw to make way for those who come after. Those who come after again make offering as before, giving way to one another. The devas and humans joyfully hear the scriptures and make music together. At that time the bliss is beyond measure. When the bodhisattvas have finished making offering and hearing the scriptures, they all rise, bow to the Buddha, and depart. They at once fly again to the places of the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below, to make offering and hear the scriptures. Each is as before, and when all is done everywhere, before the sun has reached midday each flies back to his own land. They bow to Amitabha Buddha, all withdraw and sit to hear the scriptures, and when it is done they rejoice greatly.”

The Buddha said: “When Amitabha Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats wish to eat, there are at once natural seven-treasure tables, and kalpavrksa woolen cloth is spread as seats. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas all sit before them, and all have natural seven treasures. In their bowls is food and drink of a hundred flavors, and that food and drink is like neither the world's nor the heavens'. This food and drink of a hundred flavors, throughout the eight quarters above and below, is the essence among all natural food and drink, exceedingly fragrant and fair beyond compare, born of itself by transformation. If they wish it sweet or sour, they have whatever they wish. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some wish for a golden bowl, some for a silver bowl, some for a crystal bowl, some for a red coral bowl, some for an amber bowl, some for a white jade bowl, some for a giant clam bowl, some for an agate bowl, some for a moon-bright pearl bowl, some for a mani pearl bowl, some for a purple burnished gold bowl — according to their wish it at once arrives. It comes from nowhere, and there is none who offers it; it is born of itself by transformation. The bodhisattvas and arhats all eat, and they eat neither much nor little, all equally. They do not speak of what is fine or vile, nor are they glad because it is fine. When the meal is done, the food, vessels, tables, and seats all naturally pass away by transformation. When they wish to eat again, these are again born by transformation. The bodhisattvas and arhats are all pure in heart. What they eat and drink serves only for strength; it all naturally disperses, dissolves, and passes away.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “When Amitabha Buddha expounds the scriptures for the bodhisattvas and arhats, they all assemble in the lecture hall. The bodhisattvas and arhats, with the devas and humans, countless and beyond reckoning, all fly to where Amitabha Buddha is, bow to the Buddha, and withdraw to sit and hear the scriptures. That Buddha broadly expounds the great scripture of the wisdom of the way, and all hear and know it; there is none who does not rejoice and leap up, whose heart does not open and understand. Then a natural swirling wind rises from the four quarters and blows upon the seven-treasure trees, and all give forth the five tones. The flowers of the seven-treasure trees cover that land. All come down from the empty air, and the fragrance of those flowers fills the whole land, scattering upon Amitabha Buddha and upon the bodhisattvas and arhats. The flowers fall to the ground four inches deep, and when they have slightly withered the swirling wind at once blows, and the withered flowers naturally depart. Four times the swirling wind of the four quarters blows upon the flowers of the seven-treasure trees. Then from the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, from the second heaven of Trayastrimsa up to the heaven of the Thirty-three, the devas and humans all bring ten thousand kinds of natural things from the heavens: a hundred kinds of flowers of varied colors, a hundred kinds of varied incense, a hundred kinds of variegated silk and brocade, a hundred kinds of kalpavrksa cloth garments, and ten thousand kinds of music, each surpassing the last in excellence. Each brings them down, bows to Amitabha Buddha, and makes offering to the Buddha and to the bodhisattvas and arhats. The devas and humans all again make great music, delighting Amitabha Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats. At that time the bliss cannot be told in words. The devas again give way to one another for those who come after, and those who come after again make offering as before. Then from the countless Buddha-lands of the east, their number beyond reckoning — like the flowing sands of the Ganges, one grain of sand for each Buddha, such is their number — each of those Buddhas sends bodhisattvas, countless and beyond reckoning. All fly to where Amitabha Buddha is, bow, and hear the scriptures, all rejoicing greatly. All rise, bow, and depart in like manner. The Buddhas of the west, north, and south, and of the four corners, are each in number like the flowing sands of the Ganges. Each sends countless bodhisattvas, who fly to where Amitabha Buddha is, bow, and hear the scriptures, and likewise again. Then the Buddhas below and above are each in number like the flowing sands of the Ganges. All send bodhisattvas, beyond reckoning, who fly to where Amitabha Buddha is, bow, and hear the scriptures, giving way to one another. Thus it is, and never is there a time when it ceases.”

The Buddha said: “The reason the Buddhas are numbered by the flowing sands of the Ganges is that the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below are so greatly numerous, each beyond reckoning, that they are numbered by the flowing sands of the Ganges.

The Buddha said to Ananda: “When Amitabha Buddha has finished expounding the scriptures for the bodhisattvas and arhats, among the devas and humans there are those who had not attained the way, and they at once attain the way. Those who had not attained stream-winner at once attain stream-winner. Those who had not attained once-returner at once attain once-returner. Those who had not attained non-returner at once attain non-returner. Those who had not attained arhat at once attain arhat. Those who had not attained the stage of non-retrogression at once attain the stage of non-retrogression.

Amitabha Buddha, according to the vows and delights of their seeking hearts in their former destinies, great or small as they wish, expounds the scriptures and imparts them, and at once causes them to open and understand swiftly. All are bright and wise, each delighting in what he wishes; the scriptures and the way they desire — is there any who does not rejoice in them? Those who recite and practice them recite and master them fluently, never wearied, beyond measure. Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some recite the scriptures, and their sound is like three hundred bells. Some expound the scriptures, like a swift wind and violent rain. Thus for a whole kalpa through, never is there a time of sloth or weariness. All are wise and valiant, their bodies light and nimble, never any pain or itch. At all times, walking, standing, sitting, or rising, all are able, strong, and valiant. Like the king among lions in the deep mountains, wherever he turns there is none who dares withstand him, and no thought of doubt or difficulty. What he does in his heart cannot be foreknown — by a hundred thousand billion times. And yet that fierce king among lions, by a hundred thousand billion times, is not the equal in valor of my second disciple Mahamaudgalyayana by a hundred thousand billion times. As Mahamaudgalyayana is matchless among the bodhisattvas and arhats of all those lands, flying and advancing or halting, wise and valiant, with celestial sight and celestial hearing, knowing the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present, by a hundred thousand billion times — all that wisdom joined into one — if he were made to stand beside the arhats in the land of Amitabha Buddha, his virtue would still not equal theirs by a hundred thousand billion times.”

Bodhisattva Ajita then rose, came forward, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and asked the Buddha: “Among the arhats in the land of Amitabha Buddha, are there any who have passed into parinirvana? I wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “If you wish to know, the stars of these four continents — do you see them?”
Bodhisattva Ajita said: “Yes, I see them.”

The Buddha said: “My second disciple Mahamaudgalyayana, flying up into the heavens for a single day and night, counts and knows every one of the stars. The stars of these four continents are so many that they cannot be reckoned, and yet that is a hundred thousand billion times more than the stars. If from the great ocean of the world a single drop were taken away, could it make the ocean water less, so that one knew it had diminished?”
He answered: “Take away a hundred thousand billion bushels and pecks, and still one could not know the ocean to have diminished.”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitabha Buddha, though there be arhats who have passed into parinirvana, it is as when a single drop of water is taken from the great ocean: one cannot know the arhats to have diminished.”
The Buddha said: “If a single stream of water were taken from the great ocean, would it make the ocean less?”
He answered: “Take away a hundred thousand billion streams of water, and still one could not know it to have diminished.”
The Buddha said: “If a single Ganges were taken from the great ocean, could it make the ocean less?”
He answered: “Take away a hundred thousand billion Ganges, and still one could not know it to have diminished.”

The Buddha said: “Of the arhats in the land of Amitabha Buddha, those who have passed into parinirvana are countless, and those who remain, newly attaining the way, are also countless; there is neither increase nor decrease at all.”
The Buddha said: “If all the waters of the world flowed together into the great ocean, could they make the ocean water increase?”
He answered: “They could not make it increase. Why is this? Because the great ocean is for all the waters of the world the king among all that is good, and so it is thus.”

The Buddha said: “The land of Amitabha Buddha is likewise. Though all the countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight quarters above and below go there to be born — greatly numerous, beyond reckoning — the bodhisattvas, arhats, and company of monks in the land of Amitabha Buddha remain as ever, one dharma, no different, in no way increased. Why is this? Because the land of Amitabha Buddha is the most blissful. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, it is the king among all that is good. It is the hero among Buddha-lands, the treasure among Buddha-lands; among Buddha-lands its life is the longest; it is the champion among Buddha-lands, the vastness among Buddha-lands, the capital among Buddha-lands — natural and unconditioned, most blissful, bright, and fair, a delight beyond measure. Why is this? Because when Amitabha Buddha was a bodhisattva, his vows were valiant, his striving unremitting, and this is what the piling up of virtue brought about. And so it is thus.”

Bodhisattva Ajita rejoiced greatly, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha has proclaimed the land of Amitabha Buddha — blissful, good, bright, and fair, most beautiful beyond compare — is it alone thus?”

The Buddha said: “In the land of Amitabha Buddha, among the seven-treasure dwelling places where the bodhisattvas and arhats abide, some are in the empty air and some on the ground. Some wish their dwelling to be the tallest, and their dwelling is at once tall. Some wish their dwelling to be the largest, and their dwelling is at once large. Some wish their dwelling to be in the empty air, and their dwelling is at once in the empty air — all naturally according to their thought, doing as they will. Some there are who cannot make their dwellings follow their wish. Why is this? Those who can make their dwellings follow their wish are all those who, when they sought the way in former lives and destinies, were compassionate in heart, strove diligently, and did ever more good, and this came of the weight of their virtue. Those who cannot are all those who, when they sought the way in former lives and destinies, were not compassionate in heart, did not strive diligently, and did not do ever more good, and this came of the thinness of their virtue. The clothing and food they receive is all alike, natural and equal. But their virtue is great or small, and so their valor is known apart, and this is shown to the multitude.”
The Buddha said: “Do you see the dwelling place of the king of the sixth heaven?”
Yes, I see it.”

The Buddha said: “The lecture halls and dwelling places in the land of Amitabha Buddha all surpass the dwelling place of the king of the sixth heaven by a hundred thousand billion times. The bodhisattvas and arhats all have celestial sight and celestial hearing, and see and know the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present. And the minds and thoughts of numberless devas and humans above and below, and of the winged and crawling creatures — the good and evil they think, the words they wish to speak — they know in what year and in what kalpa each shall win deliverance and attain the human way, and be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. They know who shall become bodhisattvas and arhats, and all this they foreknow. The crowns of the bodhisattvas and arhats all have light of their own. The extent of what they illumine differs; among the bodhisattvas there are two most honored, who always stand at the Buddha's right and left, seated in attendance upon the true teaching. The Buddha always sits face to face with these two bodhisattvas, deliberating the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present. If he wishes to send these two bodhisattvas to the places of the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below, they at once fly, going wherever they wish; their flight is as swift as the Buddha's, valiant beyond compare. One of these bodhisattvas is named Galevaja, and the other is named Mahasthamaprapta; in light and wisdom they are foremost. The light from their crowns blazes upon other quarters. In a thousand Buddha-lands of Mount Sumeru there is always great brightness. The light from the crowns of those bodhisattvas each illumines a thousand billion myriad li. The light from the crowns of the arhats each illumines seven zhang.”

The Buddha said: “If among the people of the world there be a good man or good woman who is in urgent fear or trouble with the authorities, let him but take refuge with these bodhisattvas Galevaja and Mahasthamaprapta, and there is none who shall not be freed.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “The light from the crown of Amitabha Buddha is a light of utmost greatness. The sun, moon, and stars all dwell in the empty air and can no longer turn and move; they have no brilliance, and their light is wholly hidden and seen no more. The Buddha's light illumines the whole land, and its blaze shines upon the Buddha-lands of other quarters, always greatly bright. Never is there a time of darkness. In that land there is no first day or second day, nor five days or ten days, nor a fifteenth day or a month, nor five months or ten months, five years or ten years, nor a hundred years or a thousand years, nor ten thousand years or a hundred million years, nor a hundred thousand million years; there is no one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a million kalpas, ten million kalpas, or a hundred billion myriad kalpas. The light of Amitabha Buddha is bright beyond measure; after countless kalpas, and countless kalpas repeated upon countless kalpas, and countless kalpas beyond number, never shall there be a time of darkness. The land and all the heavens never decay. Why is this? Because the life of Amitabha Buddha is exceedingly long and the land exceedingly good, and so it is thus. The honored life of that Buddha — after countless kalpas, and countless kalpas repeated, he has not yet come to the end of parinirvana. In the world he teaches, wishing to deliver the countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures of the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight quarters above and below, he wishes them all to be born in his land and all to attain the way of nirvana. Those who become bodhisattvas he wishes all to become Buddhas. When they have become Buddhas, they in turn teach the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures throughout the eight quarters above and below, and wish them all in turn to become Buddhas. When they have become Buddhas, they in turn teach the countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures, and cause them all to attain the way of nirvana and depart. All who can be taught as disciples, in turn teach one another and deliver one another, until they attain the ways of stream-winner, once-returner, non-returner, arhat, and pratyekabuddha, delivering one another in turn. All attain the way of nirvana, all thus. And he himself does not yet wish to enter parinirvana; those delivered by Amitabha Buddha are thus in turn. He abides again through countless kalpas, through kalpas beyond reckoning, and never is there a time of parinirvana. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, of the countless devas and humans and winged and crawling creatures born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, those who shall become Buddhas cannot be numbered; and those who become arhats and attain the way of nirvana are also countless, wholly beyond reckoning.

The kindness and virtue of Amitabha Buddha, and all that he bestows, throughout the eight quarters above and below, are without end or limit, most deep and immeasurable, blissful and good beyond words. The scriptures and the way that issue from his wisdom and teaching are proclaimed throughout the countless heavens and earths of the eight quarters above and below, most inexhaustible. The number of his scripture scrolls is exceedingly great, beyond reckoning, wholly without limit.”
The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “Do you wish to know the time of Amitabha Buddha's life without limit?”
He answered: “I wish to hear and know it.”

The Buddha said: “Listen well. Suppose all the devas and humans and winged and crawling creatures in the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight quarters above and below were all brought to enter the way, all made pratyekabuddhas and arhats, all seated in single-minded meditation, their wisdom joined into one valor, and together they wished to reckon and know the life of Amitabha Buddha — how many thousands of billions of myriads of kalpas and years it is — none could reckon or know it. And suppose again in each of a thousand Buddha-lands of Mount Sumeru in the other quarters, all the devas and humans and winged and crawling creatures were all brought to enter the way, all made pratyekabuddhas and arhats, all made to sit in single-minded meditation, their wisdom joined into one valor, and together they wished to count the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitabha Buddha, to know how many thousands of billions of myriads there are — none could know the number. The years and life of Amitabha are exceedingly long, vast and luminous, his bright goodness most deep, without limit or bottom. Who could know it and believe in it? Only the Buddha himself believes and knows it.”

Bodhisattva Ajita, hearing the Buddha's words, rejoiced greatly, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha has proclaimed that the life of Amitabha Buddha is exceedingly long, his awesome spirit honored and great, his wisdom and light towering, blissful and good — is it alone thus.”

The Buddha said: “When Amitabha Buddha at last enters parinirvana, then Bodhisattva Galevaja shall become a Buddha. He shall lead the wisdom of the way and preside over teaching. The devas and humans of the world and of the eight quarters above and below, and the winged and crawling creatures whom he delivers, shall all attain the Buddha's way of nirvana. His goodness and merit shall again be as those of the great teacher Amitabha Buddha. He shall abide through countless kalpas, through kalpas beyond reckoning. Following the great teacher as his model, he shall then enter parinirvana. After him, Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta shall in turn become a Buddha. He shall preside over wisdom and lead in teaching. The merit of what he delivers shall again be as that of the great teacher Amitabha Buddha. He shall abide through countless kalpas and shall still not enter parinirvana. Handing on the scriptures and the way in turn, most clear; the land most good — thus is the dharma. Never shall there be an end to it. It cannot be exhausted.”

Ananda knelt long, pressed his palms together, and asked the Buddha: “In the land of Amitabha Buddha there is no Mount Sumeru. On what then do the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trayastrimsa rest and abide? I wish to hear it.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “Have you any doubt concerning the Buddha? Throughout the eight quarters above and below, without end or limit, boundless and immeasurable, if all the great ocean waters of the world were measured out by one man, bushel by bushel, they could yet be dried up and their bottom mud reached — can the Buddha's wisdom be other than this?”

The Buddha said: “What I see and know of all the Buddhas of the past who bore my name, Sakyamuni — they are again like the flowing sands of the Ganges, one grain of sand for each Buddha. The Buddhas to come who shall bear my name are likewise like the flowing sands of the Ganges. Those who are only now first seeking to become Buddhas and shall bear my name are likewise like the flowing sands of the Ganges. The Buddha sits facing directly south and sees the south. The Buddhas now present who bear my name are again like the flowing sands of the Ganges. The Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, past, future, and present, who bear my name, are each like ten Ganges' flowing sands, one grain of sand for each Buddha — such is their number. The Buddha foreknows them all.”

The Buddha said: “From ages past, through numberless kalpas, in one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad kalpas, there are Buddhas. Of all the Buddhas past — one Buddha, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad Buddhas — each has a different name, and there is none who bears my name. In the kalpas just now to come, in one kalpa, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad kalpas, there are Buddhas: one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad Buddhas, each with a different name, and only now and then is there one Buddha who bears my name. Throughout the countless Buddha-lands of the eight quarters above and below, the Buddhas now present — in this other land and that, in one Buddha-land, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a hundred billion myriad Buddha-lands there are Buddhas, each with his own name, many and all different; there is none who bears my name. Among the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, only now and then is there one who bears my name. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, past, future, and present, the space between them is vast and far, distant and remote, without end or limit; the Buddha's wisdom is broad and most clear, searching out antiquity and knowing the present, knowing what is past beyond limit and beholding what is not yet, foreknowing beyond measure, wholly beyond reckoning. The countless Buddhas, their awesome spirit, honor, and brightness — he knows them all. The Buddha's wisdom and virtue are one light; there is none who can ask the Buddha to the limit of the scriptures and the way, and the Buddha's wisdom can never be measured to its end.”
Ananda heard the Buddha's words and was greatly afraid, and the hair on his body stood on end.

He said to the Buddha: “I dare not have doubt concerning the Buddha. The reason I asked the Buddha is that in the Buddha-lands of other quarters there is everywhere a Mount Sumeru, and the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trayastrimsa all rest and abide upon it. I feared that after the Buddha enters parinirvana, there might be devas and humans, or monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen, who would come and ask me: In the land of Amitabha Buddha, why alone is there no Mount Sumeru? On what do the first heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings and the second heaven of Trayastrimsa rest and abide? I should have to answer them. If I do not ask the Buddha now, after the Buddha has gone, with what words shall I reply? Only the Buddha himself knows this; no other can explain it for me. For this reason I asked the Buddha.”
The Buddha said to Ananda: “The third heaven of Yama, the fourth heaven of Tusita, up to the seventh heaven of Brahma — on what do they all rest and abide?”

Ananda said: “All those heavens naturally dwell in the empty air. They abide in the empty air, resting on nothing. The Buddha's awesome spirit is most weighty: whatever he wishes to do, he does without forethought. If all those heavens still abide in the empty air, how much more the Buddha, whose awesome spirit is honored and weighty, in whatever he wishes to do?”

Ananda heard the Buddha's words and rejoiced greatly, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha's wisdom knows the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present, without end or limit, without bound or edge, most lofty, great, wonderful, and utterly blissful, most bright and fair beyond compare. His awesome spirit is honored and weighty, not to be withstood.”

blocks.text: Sutra of Amitabha, the Truly Enlightened One of the Sagely Lineage, Delivering Beings of the Human Path, Scroll the Lower

inline.s: The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “Among the people of the world, good men and good women who wish to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha are of three grades, and the virtue they do is great or small, so that they do not reach one another.”

The Buddha said: “What are the three grades? The foremost, the first grade: one should leave home, forsake wife and children, and cut off the desires of love. One should live as a renunciant and enter the way of non-doing. One should walk the bodhisattva-way and practice the scriptures of the six paramitas. As a renunciant one should not fail in the precepts; compassionate in heart, one should strive diligently and not give way to anger. One should not have dealings with women; one should observe the fasts purely and cleanly, with a heart that covets nothing. With utmost sincerity one should wish to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. If one thinks of it constantly with a whole heart, never breaking it off, then in this present life, while seeking the way, one will naturally see Amitabha Buddha and the bodhisattvas and arhats in one's sleep and dreams. When such a person's life is about to end, Amitabha Buddha himself, with the bodhisattvas and arhats, will fly together to welcome him, and he will be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. There, in a pool of seven treasures, he will be born by transformation in a lotus flower, and will at once naturally receive a body that grows up. He will become a bodhisattva of non-retrogression, and with the bodhisattvas will fly in company and make offering to the countless Buddhas throughout the eight quarters above and below. He will at once attain wisdom and valor, delight in hearing the scriptures and the way, and his heart will rejoice. The seven-treasure dwelling he inhabits is in the empty air, and he does as he wills and wishes, near to Amitabha Buddha.”

The Buddha said: “Those who wish to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha should strive diligently, keep the scriptures and precepts, and practice the excellent dharma as above. Then they shall be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, and shall be honored by the multitude. This is the foremost, the first grade.”

The Buddha said: “The middle grade: one who wishes to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, though he cannot leave home, forsake wife and children, cut off the desires of love, and live as a renunciant, should yet hold the scriptures and precepts without failing in them. He should give more in charity and generosity, always faithfully receive the Buddha's words, and with deep sincerity hold to genuine faith. He should feed renunciants, build temples and raise stupas, scatter flowers, burn incense, light lamps, and hang variegated silk and brocade. In such dharmas he should have no preference or aversion. He should not give way to anger; he should observe the fasts purely and cleanly. Compassionate in heart, he should strive diligently and cut off the thoughts of desire. If, wishing to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, he does not break it off for a day and a night, then in this present life, too, he will see Amitabha Buddha in his sleep and dreams. When his life is about to end, Amitabha Buddha will manifest a transformation, causing him to see Amitabha Buddha and his land with his own eyes. Being born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, he may attain wisdom and valor.”

The Buddha said: “One who practices giving and charity thus, if afterward he should regret it in mid-course and doubt in his heart, not believing that giving in charity and doing good will bring blessing in a later life, not believing that there is a land of Amitabha Buddha, not believing that one may be born in that land — yet even so, if he continues to think of it without breaking off, now believing and now not believing, his will wavering with nothing to rest on, still, because he continues his good vow as his foundation, he shall be born there. When his life is about to end in sickness, Amitabha Buddha himself manifests a transformed image and causes him to see it with his own eyes. He can no longer speak, but in his heart he rejoices and leaps up, thinking: “I repent that I did not know to observe the fasts more and do good; now I shall be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha.” Such a person at once repents in his heart, and by his repentance his fault is somewhat lessened, though there is much he can no longer make up for. When his life comes to its end, he is at once born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. He cannot come before Amitabha Buddha, but on the way he sees, at the border of the land of Amitabha Buddha, a natural city of seven treasures, and his heart rejoices greatly, and he stops within that city. There, in a pool of seven treasures, he is born by transformation in a lotus flower, and receives a body that naturally grows up within the city. There he remains five hundred years. The city is two thousand li in length and breadth, and within the city there are also seven-treasure dwelling places, with seven-treasure bathing pools within and without. In the bathing pools there is also natural flower fragrance encircling them, and above the bathing pools there are also seven-treasure trees in many rows, all again giving forth the five tones. When he wishes to eat, natural food is before him, furnished with food of a hundred flavors, and whatever he wishes for comes according to his thought. Such a person is happy in the city as well, for within that city it is like the natural things of the second heaven of Trayastrimsa. Yet even so, he cannot get out of that city, and cannot see Amitabha Buddha. He sees only his light, and in his heart reproaches himself and repents, rejoicing and glad. Nor can he hear the scriptures, nor see the company of monks, nor see and know what the bodhisattvas and arhats in the land of Amitabha Buddha are like in appearance. Such a person is grieved, and this is but a small comfort to him. The Buddha does not cause such a one to obtain by his own bodily deeds what comes naturally; it is all the heart's own turning toward the way that brings him into that city. When this person sought the way in his former destiny, his heart and mouth were at variance, and his words and thoughts had no sincerity or trust. He doubted the Buddha's scriptures and did not believe in them, and so he naturally entered the evil paths; Amitabha Buddha, in pity, drew him out by his awesome spirit. Such a person must remain in that city five hundred years before he can come out. When he comes before Amitabha Buddha and hears the scriptures, his heart does not open and understand, and he is not permitted to hear the scriptures among the bodhisattvas, arhats, and company of monks. Because the dwelling he inhabits is on the ground, he cannot make his dwelling tall and lofty in the empty air at will. And he is very far from Amitabha Buddha, and cannot come near to him. His wisdom is not bright, and he knows few scriptures; his heart is not glad, and his mind does not open and understand. Yet in time he too shall of himself open and understand in wisdom and know the scriptures. Bright, strong, and valiant, his heart shall rejoice, and he shall next become as the first grade above. Why is this? Because when he sought the way in former lives and destinies, he did not much observe the fasts and precepts, and destroyed and lost the scriptures and the dharma. His will doubted, he did not believe the Buddha's words, did not deeply believe the Buddha's scriptures, did not believe that giving in charity and doing good would bring blessing in a later life. And again he regretted it in mid-course, not believing that he would be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, and his virtue was not done with a whole heart. For this reason it is thus. This is the second, the middle grade.”

The Buddha said: “The third grade: one who wishes to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, though he has no means for charity and generosity, and cannot burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, hang variegated silk and brocade, build temples, raise stupas, or feed renunciants, should yet cut off the desires of love, covet nothing, take up the scriptures swiftly, be compassionate in heart and strive diligently, not give way to anger, and observe the fasts purely and cleanly. In such dharmas he should single-mindedly think and wish to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, and if for ten days and nights he does not break it off, then when his life ends he shall at once be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. He may attain honor, wisdom, and valor.”

The Buddha said: “After one has done thus, if he again regrets it in mid-course and his heart doubts, not believing that doing good will bring blessing in a later life, not believing that he will be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha — yet even so, he shall still be born there. When his life is about to end in sickness, Amitabha Buddha causes him, in his sleep and dreams, to see the land of Amitabha Buddha. His heart rejoices greatly, and he thinks within himself: “I repent that I did not know to do more good; now I shall be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha.” This alone he thinks; he can no longer speak, and at once repents. By his repentance his fault is lessened, though there is much he can no longer make up for. When his life ends, he is at once born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. He cannot come before it, but on the way he sees a city of seven treasures two thousand li across, and his heart alone rejoices, and he stops within it. There, too, in a seven-treasure bathing pool, he is born by transformation in a lotus flower, and at once naturally receives a body that grows up. That city is also as the former city was, like the natural things of the second heaven of Trayastrimsa; and this person, too, must remain in the city until five hundred years are done before he can come out. When he comes to where Amitabha Buddha is, his heart rejoices greatly; but when he hears the scriptures, his heart does not open and understand, his mind is not glad, his wisdom is not bright, and he knows few scriptures. The dwelling he inhabits is on the ground, and he cannot make his dwelling tall and lofty in the empty air at will. And he is very far from Amitabha Buddha, and cannot come near to him. Thus it is again. This is the doubter of the second, middle grade: in time he too shall open and understand in wisdom, know the scriptures, be valiant, and have a joyful heart, and shall next become as the first grade above. Why is this? It is all because when he sought the way in former lives and destinies he regretted it in mid-course and doubted, believing and not believing by turns. Not believing that doing good brings merit and blessing, he nonetheless obtains it all naturally. According to his merit and virtue, whether he grasps it or not, each naturally turns to his own course. In expounding the scriptures and walking the way, they are a myriad billion times apart and do not reach one another.”

The Buddha said: “Those who wish to seek the bodhisattva-way and be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha shall all afterward attain to bodhisattvahood of non-retrogression. Bodhisattvas of non-retrogression shall all have the thirty-two marks, a purple burnished golden color, and the eighty minor marks. They shall all become Buddhas, according to their vows and wherever they wish. They shall become Buddhas in the Buddha-lands of other quarters, and never again pass through hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. According to their diligence in seeking the way, whether sooner or later, the matter is the same for all. If they seek the way without rest, they shall surely attain it, and shall not lose what they have vowed and wished.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “Devas, kings, and people, I tell you all: those who wish to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, though they cannot greatly strive in meditation and hold the scriptures and precepts, must in sum do good:

First, one must not take life. Second, one must not steal. Third, one must not commit lewdness or lust after the wives of others. Fourth, one must not deceive. Fifth, one must not drink wine. Sixth, one must not speak with a double tongue. Seventh, one must not speak harshly. Eighth, one must not speak falsely. Ninth, one must not envy. Tenth, one must not be greedy and gluttonous. One must not be stingy in heart, must not give way to anger, must not be foolish, must not indulge the appetites at will, must not regret in heart, must not doubt. One should be filial and obedient, should be utterly sincere and faithful, should faithfully receive the Buddha's words, and should deeply believe that doing good brings blessing in a later life. Those who uphold and practice this and do not fail in the dharma may, according to the wish of their hearts, be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. Above all one should keep the fasts and be single-minded and pure. Thinking of it day and night, wishing to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, for ten days and ten nights without breaking it off — I in my compassion pity them all, and cause them all to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha.”

The Buddha said: “People of the world who by their wishes aspire to worth and wisdom, and who live at home practicing good and walking the way, dwelling together with wife and children amid the bonds of affection and desire, are beset by many cares and household affairs in confusion, and have no leisure for great fasts and single-minded purity. Though they cannot leave home and cast off desire, yet when they have leisure they should order their own hearts and minds, think on the good their bodies may do, and single-mindedly and earnestly walk the way. If ten days and ten nights are quite impossible, let them think and weigh the matter carefully for themselves, if they wish to deliver their bodies. At the least they should cut off thought and put away care, not think on household affairs, and not share a bed with a woman. Let them order body and mind aright and cut off the desires of love. Single-mindedly keeping the fasts in purity, with utmost thought wishing to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, if for a day and a night they do not break it off, then when their lives end they shall all be born in that land. Born by transformation in a lotus flower in a seven-treasure bathing pool, they may attain wisdom and valor. The seven-treasure dwelling they inhabit, they do with as they will at ease, and they may become as the first grade above.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “The countless devas and humans throughout the eight quarters above and below — monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — who are born in the land of Amitabha Buddha: this great assembly all together in the waters of the seven-treasure bathing pools, every one of them seated upon a great lotus flower, all declare their own virtue and good deeds, each telling of his former destiny when he sought the way, the precepts he kept and the good dharmas he did, the beginning and end of the life he came from, the scriptures and way he delighted in, the wisdom he has of the scriptures, and the merit he has practiced. From highest to lowest, all in turn are told through. Thus one knows whether one's knowledge of the scriptures is bright or dim, one's wisdom deep or shallow, great or small, one's virtue excellent or poor, thick or thin; by the natural way one knows them apart. Talent, wisdom, vigor, and valor — the multitude look upon one another, in propriety and harmony, all rejoicing and leaping up; yet in wisdom and valor none reaches another.”

The Buddha said: “One who has done no virtue beforehand, who takes good lightly and makes sport of it, who does not believe it is so, who idles and is indolent, thinking it will serve — when the time comes and all are gathered to expound the scriptures and the way, he is naturally pressed and hard put, and his answers come late. The wisdom of the way stands out supreme and transcendent, in talent and strength most lofty; and he alone is at the margin, weak, repenting only when the matter is at hand. But when the repentance is already out, what good can come of it afterward? Only bitterness in his heart. Such is the one who envies and aspires to be their equal.”

The Buddha said: “The bodhisattvas and arhats of the land of Amitabha Buddha, and all that great assembly, naturally gather in a great meeting. They restrain their hearts and govern their minds, order their bodies and walk uprightly, sport and penetrate everywhere, follow one another in flight, going out and in company after company, making offerings without limit, joyful in heart and glad, together contemplating the scriptures and the way of practice, harmonious and long accustomed, keen and wise. Their will is like the empty air; they strive and seek their vows, and their hearts never again turn aside midway, their minds never again turn back, and never is there a time of sloth or weariness. Though they seek the way, outwardly they seem slow; inwardly they alone are swift. Vast and empty, they hit the mean exactly; within and without answering each other, naturally well ordered, restrained and upright, body and mind clean and pure, with no desire of love, nothing whatsoever coveted, no evil or blemish at all. Their vows and wishes are each settled and excellent, neither added to nor diminished. They seek the way in harmony and uprightness, not erring into crookedness, measuring themselves against the dharma of the way, following the scriptures and the rules, not daring to transgress or stumble. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, without bound or edge, at ease as they wish, they reach to the endless and limitless, all of them thus for the way — broad and vast, thinking of the way with no other thought, free of care and grief, natural and unconditioned, empty and still, at peace and without desire. Fulfilling good vows, they exhaust their hearts in seeking, holding pity and compassion, striving within and without, in full accord with propriety and righteousness, penetrating and unobstructed, harmonious and fitting, embracing within and without, delivering and liberating, able to ascend into nirvana, forever one light with virtue and the way, naturally preserving one another, the taste of delight most true, truly pure and white, their vow supreme, the stillness of purity, the joy of quiet without end, good and fair beyond compare, towering radiance, radiance shining through, open, reaching, bright, and clear. Within the natural, the marks of the natural; what is so has its root; naturally they accomplish five lights; the five lights reach to nine colors; the nine colors interweave and turn; many hundreds of thousands of changes. The naturalness of Uttarakuru naturally accomplishes the seven treasures, and gathering them across makes the ten thousand things; the essence of light, interwoven and bright, all issues fair, most beautiful beyond measure. If that land is thus, why not strive to do good, and think on the naturalness of the way? Fix your will above and below, penetrate without bound or edge, cast your aim into the empty air. Why does each not strive, and exert himself to seek? You may attain transcendence and depart. Be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, cut across the five evil paths; naturally they are closed, and you ascend the way without limit — easy to go, yet there is none who goes. That land does not oppose or defy; it naturally draws one along. Why not cast off the affairs of the world, practice and seek the way of virtue, and attain utmost long life, a life without end? Why cling to the affairs of the world, and with endless chatter share in anxious thoughts of impermanence? The people of the world are shallow and common; they contend together over matters that are not urgent, together here amid the utmost evil and bitterest suffering. They toil body and mind to make a living, to keep one another alive. No honored, no lowly; no rich, no poor; no old, no young; no man, no woman — all must worry together over wealth, and whether they have it or not, it is the same: their anxious thoughts are exactly equal.
