Distressed and wretched, piling up thoughts and cares. Driven by the mind, they never have a time of rest. He who has fields worries over fields; he who has a house worries over the house. He who has oxen worries over oxen; he who has horses worries over horses. He who has the six kinds of livestock worries over them. He who has servants worries over servants. He who has clothing, wealth, gold, silver, and treasures worries over them too. Thoughts heaped up, breath upon breath, worry, care, grief, and fear. Suddenly come the unforeseen: flood and fire, robbers and thieves, creditors and debtors, drowning and burning and binding, sudden assault and sinking. The poison of care is dull and heavy, and never is there a time of release. Wrath knotted in the breast, breath stored up in anger. Sickness in chest and belly, and sorrow that never leaves. The heart hard and the will firm, and no letting go at all. Some are broken and laid low, and lose their lives for good. They cast all away and go; there is none who follows them. Honored and lowly, noble and rich, poor and humble — all have these fears. Toiling thus, they bind up all manner of chills and fevers and dwell together with pain. The poor of small households, in want and hardship, lacking. He who has no fields worries and wishes for fields; he who has no house worries and wishes for a house; he who has no oxen worries and wishes for oxen; he who has no horses worries and wishes for horses; he who has none of the six livestock worries and wishes for them; he who has no servants worries and wishes for servants; he who has no clothing, wealth, goods, food and drink and the like worries and wishes to have them. No sooner has he one thing than he lacks another; having this and lacking that, he thinks to have them all equal. No sooner has he a little than it is all taken away again. Thus he lives in bitterness and must seek again. His thoughts profit him nothing, and he cannot get what he wants in time. Body and mind both toil, and sitting or rising he has no peace. Care follows upon care, and his toil is thus. Scorched heart that never leaves him, and wrath and hate and solitary rage. He too binds up all manner of chills and fevers and dwells together with pain. Sometimes for this he loses his life early, and still he will not do good or walk the way. When his life is ended and he dies, he must go far away alone. Whither he goes, and whether the path be good or evil, none can know. Sometimes people of the world, fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, households and kin within and without, dwelling between heaven and earth, ought to respect and love one another, and not hate one another; in having or lacking they ought to give to one another, and not be greedy and grudging; in word and countenance they ought to be harmonious, and not contend. If perchance their hearts contend and anger arises, the hatred of this life, the small envies and hates, in later lives grow worse and become great enmity. Why is this? As matters stand now, they wish to harm one another; though they do not at the moment break one another in sudden anger, yet the poison of grief and the wrath knotted in the spirit are naturally marked and known, and cannot be parted. Each must be born facing the other, and meet and take revenge in turn. A person in the world, amid the desires of love, goes alone and comes alone, dies alone and is born alone. When he comes to a place of suffering or of joy, he must bear it himself; there is none to take his place. Good and evil change, and calamity and evil places await him, prepared long beforehand; he must ascend alone and go far to another place, and none can see where he has gone. Good and evil naturally follow him as he goes and is born. Dark and obscure, the parting is long. The roads differ, and there is no time of meeting. It is very hard to meet again. Why not cast off household affairs, each while strong and well, strive to do good, and with all your strength seek deliverance from the world, and attain utmost long life? Yet you will not seek the way; what delight do you wait for and desire?”

People such as these do not believe that doing good brings good, do not believe that walking the way attains the way, do not believe that after death one is born again in a later world, do not believe that giving in charity brings merit and blessing; they believe none of it. They say it is not so, that there is no such thing at all; and so they see only for themselves, and pass the word from one to another, one after another, receiving it in turn. The father's leftover teaching: the ancestors and grandfathers did no good and never walked the way. Dull in body and dark in spirit, their hearts stopped up and their minds closed, they did not see the great way, and had no ability at all. Seeing people die and be born and go to some place, they could not know it either. Since they had not seen the way of good and evil, and had none to tell them, how could they do good or evil, merit or blessing, receive calamity or punishment? Each contended to do as he pleased, and none found it strange at all. And so the way of death and birth is handed on and stands from one to another. Sometimes a child weeps for a father, sometimes a father weeps for a child; sometimes a younger brother weeps for an elder, sometimes an elder weeps for a younger; sometimes a wife weeps for a husband, sometimes a husband weeps for a wife. Upside down and topsy-turvy, impermanence is the root of it, and all must pass away and cannot be kept forever. Teaching and guiding them, few believe the way. All must die and be born, and there is no rest. People such as these are dim and dull and obstinate. They do not believe the words of the scriptures, and each wishes to please himself. Their hearts take no thought. They are foolish in the desires of love and do not understand virtue and the way. They are deluded by anger and ravenous for wealth and beauty. For this they do not attain the way, and must toil more bitterly. Born at the utmost in evil places, they never find rest or cease; their suffering is most pitiable. Sometimes within a household and kin, fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, at the meaning of death and birth weep over one another and long for one another in turn. Care and grief knit together, and the bonds of affection wind on and on. Heart and mind cling to pain, and they look upon one another with longing. Day and night they are bound and obstructed, and never is there a time of release. Taught to look to virtue and the way, their hearts do not open and brighten. They think on affection and fondness, and the desires of love do not leave them. Closed and blinded, crossed and covered over. They cannot think or reckon. If the heart would order itself aright and cut through the affairs of the world, and single-mindedly and earnestly walk the way, turning at once to the very end — when life ends and the breath is gone, they cannot attain the way. What is to be done? All in a muddle and clamor, all greedy for the desires of love. In such a dharma as this, those who do not understand the way are many and those who attain it are few. The world hurries on, and there is nothing to rely on. Honored and lowly, high and low, noble and rich, poor and humble, men and women, great and small, each hurries about his own affairs, toiling and bowing his body, cherishing the poison of killing. Evil breath dark and dim, and none but is sorrowful. They do things recklessly and defy heaven and earth. They do not follow the human heart, and virtue is not evil. First it is granted them, and they are let do as they will. Before their time of life has come, it is snatched from them at a stroke. They go down into the evil paths and toil through life after life. Turning and turning in the poison of grief for many thousands of myriads of billions of years, with no time of rest — a pain beyond words, most pitiable.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the devas, kings, and people: “I tell you all: people who do the affairs of the world — for this reason they do not attain the way. Think it over well, all of you: what is evil you should let go, abandon, and turn away from. What is good you should firmly hold, and not recklessly do what is not right. Do ever more good, great or small, much or little; the glory of the desires of love can never be kept forever. It must part, and there is nothing to delight in. While the Buddha is in the world, those who faithfully receive the Buddha's words deeply and practice virtue and the way are all my younger brothers. Those who wish to begin learning the Buddha's scriptures and precepts are all my disciples. Those who wish to leave their station, go from home, forsake wife and children, cut off wealth and beauty, and become renunciants and monks for the Buddha are all my children and grandchildren. My age is very hard to meet with. Those who wish to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha may attain wisdom and valor and be honored by the multitude. Do not follow the wishes of your heart and fail the scriptures and precepts, falling behind others. If you have any doubt and do not understand the scriptures, come forward again and ask the Buddha, and I will explain them for you.”

Bodhisattva Ajita knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha's awesome spirit is honored and weighty, and the scriptures he speaks are blissful and good. Hearing the words of the scriptures, we all take them to heart. The people of the world are truly so; there is no difference from what the Buddha has said. Now the Buddha in his compassion pities us, opens and shows the great way, and teaches the words of the living path. Ears and eyes made keen, we shall long attain deliverance, and now seem to be born anew. Hearing the Buddha's words of scripture, there is none of us who is not compassionate in heart and glad, who does not leap up and open in understanding; and the devas, kings, and people, and the winged and crawling creatures, all receive the grace, and there is none who is not freed from grief. The Buddha's words of teaching and admonition are most deep and good, without limit or bottom. What the Buddha's wisdom sees and knows — the affairs of the eight quarters above and below, of past, future, and present — has no above and no below, no bound and no edge. The Buddha is very hard to hear. We have set our compassionate hearts upon the Buddha. That we have been able to win deliverance is all because the Buddha, when he sought the way in former lives, studied and questioned with diligence and pain, and attained to clarity — the grace of his virtue covering all. The merit he practiced and the blessings of his marks tower on high; his light shines through, penetrating the void without limit, entering into nirvana, teaching and gathering the scriptures, establishing his awe and melting away all things. He moves and changes the eight quarters above and below, without end or limit. The Buddha is the teacher of dharma, honored above all the sages, and there is none who can equal the Buddha. The Buddha is the teacher of the devas, kings, and people throughout the eight quarters above and below; according to the wishes of their hearts, great or small, he causes them all to attain the way. Now that we have been able to see the Buddha and to hear the name of Amitabha Buddha, we rejoice greatly, and there is none of us who has not attained keen wisdom and understanding.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “If what you say is true and it is so, then those who have a compassionate heart toward the Buddha rejoice greatly, and should truly think on the Buddha. Only after long ages does a Buddha again appear in the world. Now I have become a Buddha in an age of suffering; the scriptures and the way I set forth teach and penetrate everywhere. They cut off doubt and set the heart upright and the conduct straight. They pull out all desires of love and cut off the root of every evil. Walking at liberty and unconstrained, I govern and gather up wisdom. The ways within and without all dharmas I grasp and hold by the guiding cords. Brightly and clearly I open and show the five paths, and decide and set right the ways of birth and death and of nirvana.”

The Buddha said: “From numberless kalpas past, through kalpas beyond reckoning, you have walked the bodhisattva-way, wishing to deliver the devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures. It is very long since you began. Those who have won the way through you are countless, and those who have reached the way of nirvana are also countless. You, and the devas, kings, and people throughout the eight quarters above and below, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen — your former destinies, through numberless kalpas past, have turned and turned within these five paths, dying and being born with wailing and lamentation. Weeping over one another, longing for one another in turn, care and grief and the poison of sorrow — a pain beyond words. To this present life, death and birth have not ceased. Only today have you met the Buddha and come together with him, and now you hear the name of Amitabha Buddha, most blissful and good. I share your joy; and you may also grow weary of the pain of birth and death. Birth is most painful, most bitter, most extreme. Growing up in years is also bitter and extreme. At death, too, there is pain and bitterness and extremity; the place of evil stench and impurity is foul, and there is nothing clean or good in it. Therefore the Buddha tells you all: you too may cut off the foul place and the evil dew. You too may set your hearts upright and your bodies straight, and do ever more good. Thus always keep within and without upright, make body and mind clean. Wash away the stains of the heart, and bind and restrain yourselves. Let within and without answer each other, in word and deed faithful and true. A person can deliver himself and, in turn, support and receive others. Pull out all desires of love, be clear and bright with a whole heart. Let your vow not turn back, and bind fast the root of the good way. Though you strive and suffer for one lifetime, it is but a moment; doing good in this life, in the next you shall be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, and your bliss shall be beyond measure. Forever one light with virtue and the way, in goodness you shall preserve one another. Forever apart from the evil paths, from the pain and itch of grief and affliction, pulling out the bitter root of all evil and toil, cutting off the desires of love and fond affection. Long living in the land of Amitabha Buddha, there is no pain or itch, no evil foul place, no toil or bitterness, no lust, anger, or folly, no care or grief or poison of sorrow. Born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, you may wish for a life of one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million kalpas. At your own will and pleasure, you may abide with a life of countless kalpas, of kalpas beyond reckoning. As you will and wish, you may have it all. To eat or not to eat, as you please. All things are natural, and you may have them all. Next to the way of nirvana, let each of you be clear and bright and seek it out. Whatever your heart wishes, do not doubt or regret in your heart. Those who wish to be born there must not, by their own fault, be set down for five hundred years in a natural city of seven treasures at the border of the land of Amitabha Buddha.”
Bodhisattva Ajita said: “We receive the Buddha's stern and lucid and weighty teaching; we shall all strive diligently and single-mindedly seek. We beg to practice it, and dare not doubt or slacken.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “If in this world you can govern your own hearts and set your minds upright, and your bodies do no evil, this is great virtue and goodness. This is a whole grade of its own, matchless throughout the eight quarters above and below. Why is this? Throughout the eight quarters above and below, in the countless Buddha-lands, the devas and humans all naturally do good and do not greatly do evil, and are easy to teach and transform. Now I have become a Buddha in this world, become a Buddha amid the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings. I teach and speak to the people in the sharpest extremity, causing them to let go the five evils, to put away the five pains, and to put away the five burnings, subduing and transforming their hearts. I cause them to hold the five goods, and to attain the merit and blessing of deliverance from the world, long life, and the way of nirvana.”

The Buddha said: “What are the five evils? What are the five pains? What are the five burnings? What is the melting away of the five evils? What is it to attain the five goods? What is it to hold the five goods, and to attain the merit and blessing of long life, and the way of deliverance from the world and nirvana?”

The Buddha said: “The first evil: devas and humans, and down to the beasts and the winged and crawling creatures, wish to do all manner of evil. The strong overpower the weak, and they plunder one another in turn. They wound and kill one another, and eat one another in turn. They do not know to do good, and are evil and defiant and without the way. They receive their calamity and punishment, for such is the natural way of things. Where they are bound, the spirits mark and know it. Those who transgress are not forgiven, and the debt is handed on and on. Hence there are poverty and lowliness, begging and loneliness. Hence there are deafness and blindness, dumbness and folly, sullenness and evil. Below there are the crooked and the mad, and those who cannot reach what they seek. Hence there are the honored and lowly, the noble and rich, the highly gifted and clear-minded, the wise and valiant — all by their former destinies of doing good, being compassionate and filial, and bestowing kindness and virtue. Hence there are lawsuits, the king's law, and prisons. Those who will not fear and take care, who do evil and fall under the law, receive their fault and punishment, and heavy fines bring extremity. They seek release and deliverance, but it is hard to win free. In this life there is this, present before your eyes. When life ends there is a place; they enter its darkness and receive a body and are born again. It is like the king's law, with bitter suffering and utmost punishment. Hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. Their bodies change in trade, they alter their evil and change their path. Life short or long, the spirit and subtle consciousness naturally enter their course and receive a body and lodge in a womb. Each must meet what faces him, and they follow one another and are born together. They repay one another in turn, and must give back in turn. Calamity and evil, disaster and punishment — the many matters are not yet done. They can never be free, but turn and turn within them. Life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. Between heaven and earth this is naturally so. Though it is not at the moment, it comes suddenly in its season. One has only to take the natural way; good and evil both return to it. This is the first great evil, the first pain, the first burning. Toil and bitterness such as this, the poison of sorrow and wailing. It is like a fierce fire rising to burn a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, and alone do all good and do no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvana. This is the first great good.”

The Buddha said: “The second evil: the kings of the world, the officials and the people, fathers and sons, brothers, households, husbands and wives, are almost wholly without propriety or reason. They do not follow the upright commands, but are extravagant, lewd, and arrogant. Each wishes to please himself and do as his heart pleases. They cheat and mock one another, and have no fear of death at all. Heart and mouth differ, and their words and thoughts are untrue. Flattering and fawning, disloyal, wheedling and cunning in speech. Their conduct has no order; they envy and hate one another, slander and speak evil of one another in turn, and ensnare people in false charges. The ruler is not clear-minded, his heart does not examine and illumine, and he employs his ministers. The ministers, being in place, tread and measure what they can do. Knowing how to shape and apply things, they sit in their seats without uprightness. Being mocked by them, he recklessly damages the loyal and good and worthy and virtuous. This does not accord with the heart of heaven, and greatly violates reason. The minister cheats his lord, the son cheats his father. The younger brother cheats the elder, the wife cheats the husband. Within the household and without, friends and acquaintances sue one another. Each harbors greed and lust, a heart of poison and anger, and in blind folly and ignorance wishes to increase himself. There is no honored or lowly, high or low; no man, no woman; no great, no small. Their hearts are all alike, each wishing to enrich himself. They ruin their households and destroy themselves, with no thought of those before or after. Household and kin are broken and their clan destroyed by it. Sometimes within the household and without, friends and acquaintances, the village and the marketplace, foolish folk and rustics, turn to one another's affairs, each seeking his own gain and harm. They contend over wealth and fight lawsuits, and wrath and rage become enmity, and they contend in turn for victory and defeat. The rich and stingy scorch their hearts and will not give in charity. Grudging and guarding what they love, clinging to it and hoarding it. For this they brood, and their hearts toil and their bodies suffer. Thus to the very end, with nothing to rely on. They come alone and go alone, and not one follows them. Good and evil, merit and blessing, calamity and punishment follow the life they go to; some are in a place of bliss, some enter poison and suffering. Only then do they repent — but what use is that? Sometimes people of the world, foolish in heart and scant of wisdom, seeing the good, slander and hate them, and will not aspire to follow. They wish only to do reckless and wayless things, wish only to steal, always harboring a poisonous heart. They wish to get the wealth of others to supply themselves. When it is scattered and spent, they seek it again. Their crooked hearts are not upright, and they are always alone in terror, fearing the countenance of others. At the moment they take no thought, and only when the matter comes do they repent. In this present life, the officials and the prisons — they naturally turn their course and receive their calamity. The poverty, begging, and loneliness of the world come only from former destinies. Not believing in virtue and the way, unwilling to do good, doing evil in this life, the devas record them in a separate register. When life ends they enter the evil paths; hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. They turn and turn within them. Life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, there is no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. This is the second great evil. The second pain, the second burning — toil and bitterness such as this. It is like a fire rising, fiercer than burning a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, and alone do all good and do no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvana. This is the second great good.”

The Buddha said: “The third evil: the people of the world, dwelling as parasites upon one another, live together between heaven and earth, and the years of their lives — how many can there be? There are the noble and rich and elders, the wise and good; below them the poor and lowly, the crooked and weak, the foolish. Among them are wicked people who only harbor poison and evil in their thoughts, whose bodies and minds are not upright. They always think on lust, and their breasts are full and troubled. Desires of love cross and tangle, and sitting or rising they have no peace. Their greedy minds are stingy, and they wish to seize and get by force. They leer at fine forms, with evil manner and lust. Hating and loathing their own wives, they go secretly in and out on their own. They take what the household has and give it to wrongdoing. They gather to eat and drink, and together devote themselves to evil. They raise troops and turn bandit, attack cities and fight duels. They rob and kill and cut off, and seize by force without the way. Taking the wealth of others, stealing to get what they want, unwilling to make an honest living. What they ought to seek, they will not do. Their evil minds are set abroad and cannot be single in their work. Wishing to bind things into accomplishment, they use threats and force. They bring it home to supply the household, to live on together. They give their hearts free rein and take their pleasure, going to the utmost in revelry. They violate the wives of others, and do not shrink even from their own kin; the honored and lowly and the elders all hate and loathe them. Within the household and without, they are afflicted and angered by them. Nor do they fear the officials and the law, and there is nothing they avoid or take account of. For evil such as this, naturally there are prisons. Sun and moon shine and know it, the spirits mark and take it down, the gods seize and record it; hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. They turn and turn within them, life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, with no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. This is the third great evil, the third pain, the third burning. Toil and bitterness such as this are like a fire rising to burn a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, and alone do all good and do no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvana. This is the third great good.”

The Buddha said: “The fourth evil: people cannot do good, and ruin one another. They teach and command one another, and together do all manner of evil. Their chief business is to carry tales; they wish only for a double tongue, harsh speech, abuse, and lies. They envy and stir up strife against one another. They hate and envy the good, and ruin the worthy and virtuous. They take pleasure in it on the side, and are not filial or dutiful, nor do they support their parents. They make light of teachers, friends, and acquaintances, and are without trust and hard to make honest. They think themselves great and honored; they have a way of going about in force and might, adding power and authority. They encroach upon and mistreat others, and cannot know themselves; doing evil, they are not ashamed, but rely on their own stubborn strength. They wish people to serve and fear and respect them. Yet they do not fear or respect heaven and earth, the spirits, the sun and moon. Nor can they be taught or commanded to do good, nor be subdued and transformed; they rely on themselves and are proud, and think it must always be so. Nor have they any heart of grief or pity, nor know the meaning of fear. Arrogant as they are, the devas mark them. Relying on their former destinies, they have done some merit and virtue. A little good supports and receives them, guards and helps them. Doing evil in this life, they exhaust all their good, and day by day it departs. They see evil and go after it; they stand alone and empty, with nothing more to rely on, and receive heavy calamity and punishment. When life ends, all evils gather around them. Naturally pressed and hard put, they must go in pursuit, and cannot rest. Naturally all evils together drive them to exhaustion. Their names are recorded in the register of the spirits. Calamity draws and pulls them, and they must meet what they have earned. Naturally they turn their course, and receive their punishment. Body and mind are shattered, spirit and form in utmost suffering, and they cannot get away. They can only go forward, and enter the cauldron of fire. At that time, what use is repentance? What can they do? The way of heaven is natural, and none can stumble aside. Hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures; they turn and turn within them, life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, with no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. This is the fourth great evil, the fourth pain, the fourth burning. Toil and bitterness such as this are like a fire rising to burn a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, and alone do all good and do no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvana. This is the fourth great good.”

The Buddha said: “The fifth evil: people of the world idle and are lazy, unwilling to do good, and do not think to make a living. Their wives and children go hungry and cold, and their parents likewise. When they wish to scold and teach their children, their children's hearts are evil. They glare and answer in anger, and will not obey their words. Defiant and rebellious, worse than the wild folk. Like enemies, better to have had no children at all. They borrow and lend recklessly, and all are afflicted and sick of it. There is especially no thought of repaying. Impoverished and in want, they cannot get again. They lay snares and make fair sounds, give themselves up to wandering and scattering. Habitually they get things for nothing, and use them to relieve themselves, with no fear of the prohibitions. In food and drink they know no limit, drinking wine and craving delicacies. Their coming and going has no set time; rude and reckless, they knock against everything. They do not know human feeling, and force and compel with shouts. Seeing others happy, they hate and envy and rage at them. Without righteousness or propriety, self-willed in judging what is right, past all remonstrance. They do not grieve over whether their parents, wives, and children have anything or not, nor think to repay their parents' kindness, nor think on the goodness of their teachers. Their hearts always think evil, their mouths always speak evil, their bodies always do evil, and day by day they accomplish nothing. They do not believe in virtue and the way, do not believe there are wise and worthy sages of old, do not believe that doing good and walking the way can deliver one from the world, do not believe that there is a Buddha in the world. They wish to kill arhats, to set the company of monks at odds, always to kill people, to kill their parents, brothers, wives, children, kin, and friends. Their parents, brothers, wives, children, kin, and friends hate and loathe the sight of them, and wish them dead. They do not believe the Buddha's words of scripture, do not believe that a person's life comes to an end, that after death one is born again in a later world. They do not believe that doing good brings good, nor that doing evil brings evil. Men and women such as these, their hearts all alike, defiant and rebellious. Foolish and blind, angry and craving, knowing nothing at all. They think themselves happy and good, and greatly wise. They do not know whence they come, nor where birth and death are bound. They will not be kind or filial, and defy heaven and earth. In the meantime they hope for luck. They wish for long life, and call upon death not to come. But they must go to it at last — the toil and bitterness of birth and death, the ways of good and evil. The evil their bodies have done, the calamities and all their courses, they cannot win free of. Nor can they be subdued and transformed and made to do good. With a compassionate heart one teaches and speaks, opening and guiding them through the suffering of death. Whither good and evil lead — they do not believe even this. Yet with bitter heart one speaks to them, wishing to deliver them, and it profits them nothing. Their hearts are closed up and their minds do not open and understand. The great command is about to come, and at that time they all repent. Repenting afterward — what can they do? Not having planned beforehand to do good, what use is it in extremity? Between heaven and earth the five paths are each distinct. Vast and deep, wide and boundless. They receive in turn, good and evil, poison and pain. Each must bear it himself, and there is none to take his place. The way is natural, and follows what one has done. It pursues the life one goes to, and one cannot let it go. The good do good, are compassionate and filial, and go from bliss into bliss, from light into light. The evil do evil, and go from suffering to darkness; who can know them? Only the Buddha sees and knows. Teaching and speaking to the people, few believe and accept. Birth and death do not cease, and the evil paths are not cut off. People such as these cannot all be told of. Hence there are the natural hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. They turn and turn within them, life after life, kalpa piled on kalpa, with no time of escape. Deliverance is hard to win, and the pain is beyond words. This is the fifth great evil, the five pains, the five burnings; toil and bitterness such as this are like a fire rising to burn a man's body. If a person can within this single-mindedly govern his mind, set his body upright and walk straight, let word and deed answer each other, and make all he does utterly sincere. Let his words be as they are, his heart and mouth not turning. Alone doing all good and doing no evil, then he alone is delivered and wins merit and blessing. He may attain long life, deliverance from the world, ascent to the heavens, and the way of nirvana. This is the fifth great good.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “I tell you all: the five evils of this world, and the toil and bitterness that are thus. They give rise to the five pains, give rise to the five burnings, and beget one another in turn. The people of the world will not do good. Those who wish to do all manner of evil and dare to commit these evil things shall all naturally pass through and enter the evil paths. Some in this life first suffer sickness and calamity, and in death and birth find no relief; they are shown to the multitude. When life ends they go to the utmost suffering, grief, and cruel poison. They scorch one another and burn one another away. After that they become enemies together and wound and kill one another. From the smallest beginning it grows to great extremity. It all comes of greed and lust for wealth and beauty, of unwillingness to bear insult, and of each wishing to please himself in what he gives. There is no more right or wrong, only the wish for a strong name. Driven by foolish craving and following the thoughts of the heart, they cannot get what they want, and wrath is knotted in their breasts. Bound by wealth and beauty, with no release, knowing no contentment. Enriching themselves and contending in desire, taking no account of anything. Wealth and honor and glory — if at the time one could bear insult and did not know to do good in charity. Power lasts but a little, and one is scorched along with an evil name. The body sits in toil and bitterness, and after a long time comes great extremity. Naturally it follows and pursues, and there is no release. The king's law is spread abroad, and naturally impeaches and seizes them. Above and below answer one another, a net of rule and order. Alone and afraid, they must enter it. From ancient times to now this has been so — how pitiable and grievous. Wholly without reason or propriety, not knowing the upright way.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “When a Buddha such as this is in the world, in his compassion and pity, the awe of his spirit shakes and moves them. All evil things are melted away and transformed. He causes them to leave evil and draw near to good, and to cast off what they think. Upholding the scriptures and precepts, there is none who does not receive them. They practice the scriptures and the dharma, and dare not transgress or lose them. The way of deliverance from the world, of non-doing and nirvana, is blissful and good and of utmost joy.”

The Buddha said: “You devas, kings, and people, and the people of later ages: when you have obtained the Buddha's words of scripture, think them over well. If you can within this set your hearts upright and walk straight, and those above you do good and lead and transform and restrain those below, teaching the multitude and commanding one another in turn, together doing good and delivering one another in turn, each ordering and keeping himself, compassionate and kind and pitying, never slackening to the end of life, honoring the sages and reverencing filial piety, penetrating and loving widely — the Buddha's words and commands, let none dare fail. You should grieve for the way of deliverance from the world and nirvana; you should grieve to cut off the pain and itch of birth and death and pull out the root of evil. You should grieve to cut off the evil and bitter paths of the hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures. While the Buddha is in the world, hold firmly to the scriptures and the way, and dare not transgress or lose them.”

The Buddha said: “If you would believe, what is the first urgency? You should order your own body, order your own mind, order your own eyes, order your own ears, order your own nose, order your own mouth, order your own hands, order your own feet. If you can restrain yourselves and not act recklessly. Let body and mind be pure and clean, and both answer to good. Restrain within and without, and do not follow the appetites. Transgress no evil; let word and countenance be harmonious, and the body's conduct single. In walking, standing, sitting, or rising, let all you do be at peace. In whatever you do, first think it over carefully and reckon it. Measure your ability, look all around, and settle it calmly before you act. To act in haste, without forethought and careful reckoning, is to do it without truth, and you lose your labor. Failure and regret come after, and you toil in vain and lose yourself. Utterly sincere and faithful, you attain the way and depart.”

The Buddha said: “If you thus do ever more good, bestowing kindness and practicing virtue, and can avoid transgressing the prohibitions of the way, bearing insult and striving diligently, single-minded in wisdom, teaching one another in turn and doing good and virtue — then in such a dharma as this, with a compassionate heart and single-mindedness, keeping the fasts purely and cleanly for a day and a night, you surpass a hundred years of doing good in the land of Amitabha Buddha. Why is this? In the land of Amitabha Buddha all is accumulated virtue and a multitude of good. Unconditioned and natural, whatever one seeks is there. There is no evil at all, great as a hair.

The Buddha said: “Here, one who does good for ten days and ten nights surpasses in virtue the people of the Buddha-lands of other quarters who do good for a thousand years. Why is this? In the Buddha-lands of other quarters all do good. Those who do good are many and those who do evil are few, and all have natural things. They do not go seeking and doing, but get them of themselves. Here those who do evil are many and those who do good are few, and if one does not go seeking and doing, one cannot get them. The people of the world can order and govern themselves and do good, and with a whole heart seek the way, and so it is thus. Here there is nothing natural; one cannot supply oneself. One must go seeking, toiling bitterly to make a living. Cheating and deceiving one another in turn, tricking and feigning good and evil. Getting wealth and goods, one brings them home to wife and children. Food and drink poison the mind and weary the body with suffering. Thus to the very end. The heart and mind are not single
yi
tai
gong
xin
— that is, confused and ill at ease. If a person can quiet himself and do good and strive in virtue, then it is thus.”

The Buddha said: “I pity you all, and the devas, kings, and people. I teach and command you all to do every good and not to do any evil. According to what each can do, I at once impart the way. Teaching and admonishing and opening and guiding — all of you, practice them. Then the ruler leads and transforms to good and teaches and commands his ministers; the father teaches his son, the elder brother his younger, the husband his wife; within the household and without, kin and friends teach and speak to one another in turn. Doing good and walking the way, upholding the scriptures and keeping the precepts. Each orders and keeps himself; above and below restrain one another. No honored, no lowly; no man, no woman. Pure in the fasts, there is none who is not glad. Harmonious and reasonable, joyful and compassionate and filial, they bind and restrain one another. Those who obtain the Buddha's words of scripture all hold and think on them. What they ought not to do, if they transgress and do it, they at once repent and turn from evil and draw near to good. They cast off the crooked and make it upright, hearing in the morning and mending by evening. Upholding the scriptures and precepts, the foolish obtain a treasure. Wherever the Buddha has been, in whatever province or kingdom, he at once imparts the scriptures and precepts: to the devas, sun, moon, stars, and gods; to kings, ministers, officials, and people; to nagas, ghosts, and spirits, the hells, the beasts, the hungry ghosts, and the winged and crawling creatures — there is none who does not open in a compassionate heart. All revere and serve, and receive the scriptures and the way from the Buddha with bowed head. They receive and practice them, and the ruler at once changes and is transformed to good. Keeping the fasts, thinking with purity, washing himself clean, ordering his heart and walking straight, he sits in his place in reverence and awe. He teaches and commands and leads the multitude to good. He practices the prohibitions of the way, and makes his commands and words upright. The minister is filial to his lord, loyal and upright, receiving his commands and daring not to defy them. Father and son in their commands are dutiful and obedient. Brothers, husbands and wives, kin and friends. Above and below they command one another, obeying in harmonious reason. Honored and lowly, great and small, serve one another with respect in turn. In propriety and righteousness they do not betray one another, and all change what is past and cultivate what is to come, washing the heart and altering conduct, upright within and without. Naturally doing good, whatever they wish they at once obtain. All good subdues and transforms by the natural way. If one seeks not to die, one may obtain long life; if one seeks deliverance from the world, one may obtain the way of nirvana.”

The Buddha said: “The Buddha's awesome spirit is honored and his virtue weighty; he melts evil into good, and there is none who is not delivered. Now I have come forth into the world, here amid evil, become a Buddha in an age of suffering, in compassion and pity and grief, teaching and speaking and opening and guiding. The devas, kings, ministers and attendants about them, officials and people — according to what their hearts wish and delight in, I cause them all to attain the way. Wherever the Buddha has been, through whatever provinces, counties, towns, hamlets, and marketplaces he has passed, there is nothing that is not abundant and ripe. The world is at great peace; sun and moon move and shine, doubling their brightness and beauty. Wind and rain come in season, and the people are at rest. The strong do not oppress the weak, and each finds his place. There are no bad years or plagues, no sick or wasted folk. Weapons are not raised, and in the land there are no robbers or thieves. There are no grievances

; none are imprisoned. Rulers and ministers and people, there is none who does not rejoice and leap up. Loyal and compassionate and utterly sincere, each orders and keeps himself, and each keeps his own land. Harmonious and filial, there is none who is not glad. In having and lacking they give to one another, bestowing kindness and practicing virtue. Their hearts are glad and joyful, and all respect and love. They yield and defer in righteousness and modesty. Before and after, they serve one another with propriety. As father and son, as elder brother and younger brother, there is none who is not benevolent and worthy. Harmonious in propriety and measure, wholly without contention. Blissful and good beyond measure.”

The Buddha said: “I pity you as my children, and wish to deliver you, more than a father and mother think on their child. Now the devas, kings, and people throughout the eight quarters above and below, and the winged and crawling creatures, who obtain the Buddha's scriptures and precepts and practice the Buddha-way, all attain bright wisdom, and their hearts all open and understand; there is none who does not win deliverance from grief. Now that I have become a Buddha amid the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, I subdue and transform the five evils, melt away the five pains, and utterly extinguish the five burnings. With good I attack evil and pull out the poison and suffering. I cause them to attain the five paths, to attain the five goods, bright and fair, so that the burning evil does not arise. After I enter parinirvana, the scriptures and the way will gradually be cut off. The people will be flattering and fawning, and gradually do all manner of evil again, and no more do good. The five burnings will rise again. The five pains will be bitter in the extreme. It will be as before. Naturally it will come back again. After a long time it will grow worse, beyond all telling. I have told you only a little of the way.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the rest: “Let each of you think on this and hold it, and teach and admonish one another in turn. According to the Buddha's scriptures and dharma, let none dare transgress.”

Bodhisattva Ajita knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha's record of the way is most bitter and painful, and the people of the world do evil so greatly. The Buddha in his compassion pities them all and delivers them all. We all say that we receive the Buddha's weighty teaching. We beg to teach one another in turn. We dare not transgress.”
The Buddha said to Ananda: “In my pity for you all, I cause you all to see Amitabha Buddha and the land where the bodhisattvas and arhats dwell. Do you wish to see it?”
Ananda at once rejoiced greatly, knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “I wish to see it all.”
The Buddha said: “Rise, and put on your robe again, and bow toward the west. Where the sun sets, bow to Amitabha Buddha. With your head to the ground, say: Namo Amitabha Samyak-saṃbuddha.”

Ananda said: “Yes, I receive your teaching. Then he rose, put on his robe again, and bowed toward the west. Where the sun sets, he bowed to Amitabha Buddha. With his head to the ground, he said: Namo Amitabha Samyak-saṃbuddha.”

Before Ananda had risen, Amitabha Buddha at once sent forth the radiance and awe of his great light. It filled the eight quarters above and below, the countless Buddha-lands; and all the countless heavens and earths were at once greatly shaken. In all the countless heavens and earths, the precious Mount Sumeru and the precious Great Mount Sumeru, and the great and small boundaries of all the heavens and earths — within them the great hells and small hells, and the dark places of the mountains, forests, streams, and valleys — were at once greatly bright, all widely opened and made plain.

Then Ananda, the bodhisattvas, the arhats, and the devas, kings, and people all saw Amitabha Buddha and the seven treasures of the land of the bodhisattvas and arhats, and their hearts rejoiced and leaped up greatly. All rose and bowed to Amitabha Buddha. With their heads to the ground, they all said: Namo Amitabha Samyak-saṃbuddha.

When the land of Amitabha Buddha sent forth the radiance and awe of its light, all the countless devas and humans and the winged and crawling creatures saw the light of Amitabha Buddha, and there was none whose heart was not compassionate and glad. In all the hells, among the beasts and hungry ghosts, in every place of torment and bitter toil, all at once ceased and tormented no more, and there was none who was not freed from grief. All who were blind at once received sight. All who were deaf at once received hearing. All who were mute at once could speak. All who were bent at once were straightened. The lame, the crippled, and the halt all at once walked and ran. All who were sick at once rose healed. All who were weak at once grew strong. All who were foolish at once became wise. All who were given to lust all practiced the pure life. All who were angry all became compassionate in heart and did good. In all who had taken poison, the poison did not work. Bells and chimes, lutes and zithers, harps and konghous, instruments and all manner of music, sounded of themselves without being struck. The pearls and rings of women gave forth sound of themselves. The hundred birds and the beasts all raised their own plaintive cries. At that time there was none who did not rejoice in good bliss and win deliverance. And at that very time, all the devas and humans throughout the Buddha-lands brought down celestial flowers and incense, and in the empty air made offering to all, scattering them upon all the Buddhas and upon Amitabha Buddha. The devas each together made ten thousand kinds of spontaneous music, delighting all the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas and arhats. At that time the bliss could not be told in words.

The Buddha said to Ananda: “Ajita the bodhisattva and the rest — when I speak of Amitabha Buddha and of the bodhisattvas and arhats and the land naturally adorned with the seven treasures, is there anything that differs?”

Ananda knelt long, pressed his palms together, and said: “The Buddha has proclaimed the land of Amitabha Buddha as blissful and good; there is not one thing that differs from what the Buddha has spoken.”
The Buddha said: “Were I to tell of the merit, virtue, and excellence of the land of Amitabha Buddha, a whole kalpa of days and nights would not yet exhaust it; I have told you only a little.”

Bodhisattva Ajita at once knelt long, pressed his palms together, and asked the Buddha: “From this land of the Buddha, how many bodhisattvas of non-retrogression shall there be who are born in the land of Amitabha Buddha? I wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: “If you wish to know, listen clearly and hold it in your heart.”
Bodhisattva Ajita said: “I receive your teaching.”

The Buddha said: “From this land of mine there shall be seven hundred and twenty koṭis of bodhisattvas of non-retrogression, all to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. Each such bodhisattva of non-retrogression, having gone before and made offering to countless Buddhas in succession, shall in turn, as Maitreya does, all become Buddhas; and the rest, the lesser bodhisattvas, countless and beyond reckoning, shall all be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha.”

The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita: “Not only the bodhisattvas in my own land shall be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. In the Buddha-lands of other quarters there are also Buddhas, and it is likewise with them. The first Buddha is named Surupa; in his land there are a hundred and eighty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The second Buddha is named Ratnakara; in his land there are ninety koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The third Buddha is named Suruci; in his land there are two hundred and twenty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The fourth Buddha is named Amṛtarāja; in his land there are two hundred and fifty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The fifth Buddha is named Lobhapravaracai

The twelfth Buddha is named Vipulayanacai; in his land the bodhisattvas are countless and beyond reckoning, all of them of non-retrogression, all wise and valiant, each having made offering to countless Buddhas, and with one mind at one time all wishing to go, they shall all be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, in the Buddha-lands of other quarters. The thirteenth Buddha is named Svākṣarāvarta; in his land there are seven hundred and ninety koṭis of bodhisattvas, all to be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha.”

The Buddha said: “These bodhisattvas are all of non-retrogression; and among the company of monks, and the lesser bodhisattvas, countless in number, all shall be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. Not only the bodhisattvas of these fourteen Buddha-lands shall be born there. Throughout the eight quarters above and below, the bodhisattvas of the countless Buddha-lands, each and every one, shall all be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha. Countless beyond number, they shall all go together to the assembly in the land of Amitabha Buddha. The great multitude cannot be reckoned. Were I to tell only the names of the countless Buddhas of the eight quarters above and below, for a whole kalpa of days and nights it would not yet be done. Were I again to tell only the number of the monks and bodhisattvas in the Buddha-lands who shall be born in the land of Amitabha Buddha, telling it for a kalpa without rest, it would not yet be done. I have told you only the whole of it gathered up in little.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “Ajita the bodhisattva and the rest — the kings and people of the world, good men and good women, who by good done in former destinies have won towering blessings and honor, so that they may hear the name of Amitabha Buddha — how blissful and good; I rejoice for them.”

The Buddha said: “Those good men and good women who hear the name of Amitabha Buddha, and with a compassionate heart rejoice, leaping up at once; whose hearts and minds are pure and clean, the hair on whose bodies stands on end, and whose tears at once flow — all these have in former destinies walked the Buddha-way. Or they are bodhisattvas from other quarters, come for the sake of the Buddha, and are no ordinary people. And those people, men and women, who hear the name of Amitabha Buddha and do not believe it, who do not believe the scriptures and the Buddha's words, who do not believe there is a company of monks, whose hearts doubt and who believe nothing at all — all these have come from the evil paths to be born here. Foolish and not understanding their former destinies, their calamity and evil are not yet exhausted. Because they are not yet to be delivered, their hearts doubt and they do not believe.”

The Buddha said: “I tell you all: whatever good dharmas you ought to do, you should all practice and believe, and not doubt. After I enter parinirvana, you and the people of later ages must not again say, I do not believe there is a land of Amitabha Buddha. I have caused you all to see the land of Amitabha Buddha, and what should be done, each should seek for himself. I have fully told you the scriptures, the precepts, and the dharma of care, and you should hold them as the Buddha's dharma, and not destroy or lose them. I entrust this scripture to you all; you should firmly hold it, and not deal with it falsely, adding to or taking from this dharma of scripture. After I enter parinirvana, the scriptures and the way will remain for a thousand years. After a thousand years the scriptures and the way will be cut off; in my compassion I will keep this dharma of scripture and let it remain a hundred years. When the hundred years are done, then it will cease and be cut off. According to the wish of the heart, all may attain the way.”

The Buddha said: “A teacher opens and guides people's ears and eyes, and by wisdom and clear understanding delivers them, causing them to attain good and join the way of nirvana. One should always be filial and kind toward the Buddha and one's parents, always think on the teacher's kindness, and think of it without cease — and one shall swiftly attain the way.”
The Buddha said: “A Buddha appearing in the world is very hard to meet with. And if there be a renunciant, or a teacher who expounds the scriptures for others, he is very hard to meet with.”

When the Buddha spoke this scripture, twelve thousand koṭis of devas and humans all attained celestial sight and celestial vision, and all with one mind set out on the bodhisattva-way. Two hundred koṭis of devas and humans all attained the way of the non-returner. Eight hundred renunciants all attained the way of the arhat. Forty koṭis of bodhisattvas all attained non-retrogression.

When the Buddha had spoken the scripture, the bodhisattvas and arhats, the devas, kings, and people all rejoiced greatly, rose, bowed to the Buddha, walked around him three times, and went their way, bowing their heads to the Buddha's feet.
